covers.quote: Place a comma after adverbs and other introductory words
You don’t need a comma after an introductory word if the sentence is very short.

examples.note: Comma used after affirmative introductory word.

parts.quote: Yes, they went to the estimates hearing.

examples.note: Comma used after introductory greeting.

parts.quote: Goodnight, and good luck.

examples.note: Comma used after introductory adverb.

parts.quote: Actually, that's an interesting point.

rules.quote: Use a comma after introductory words, such as greetings and adverbs, or when addressing someone.
rules.specification: 'Very short' sentences may be interpreted as 4 or fewer words, where the introductory comma may be omitted.
rules.violation_condition: an introductory word (such as a greeting, adverb, or direct address) not followed by a comma, unless the sentence is very short
when: Sentences that begin with an introductory word (greetings, adverbs, direct address).
A comma is not needed if the sentence is very short.
rules.why: G-3 folds permission for very short sentences into when; E-4 documents resolvable length threshold.

covers.quote: Use a comma after phrases and clauses that change the whole sentence
Conditional clauses are adverbial clauses (for example, beginning with ‘if’, ‘unless’ or ‘until’). They should also have a comma after them if they start the sentence.
In these cases, you don’t need a comma before the phrase.

examples.note: Comma used after introductory adverbial phrase.

parts.quote: During the meeting, we discussed Item 9.

examples.note: No comma needed when adverbial phrase is placed at the end of the sentence.

parts.quote: We discussed Item 9 during the meeting.

examples.note: Adverbial clause at start of sentence followed by comma.

parts.quote: Although they were shaking and sweating, the firefighters were relieved to feel the first drops of a downpour.

examples.note: Conditional adverbial clause at start of sentence followed by comma.

parts.quote: Unless the consultation starts early, it will not finish on time.

rules.quote: Use commas after adverbial phrases and adverbial clauses.
rules.violation_condition: an introductory adverbial phrase or clause (including conditional clauses) starting a sentence without a following comma
when: The adverbial phrase or clause starts the sentence.
A comma is not needed before the phrase if it is moved to the end of the sentence.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates conditional clauses as adverbial clauses; G-3 records clause-at-end relaxation under when.

covers.quote: Use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral. It doesn’t matter how short the sentence is.
Avoid this type of sentence structure because the string of numbers can be confusing.

examples.note: Sentence structured to avoid stringing a date and number together at the beginning.

parts.quote: There were 16.5 million people enrolled to vote in Australian elections on 18 April 2019.

examples.note: Begins with a date followed immediately by another numeral.

parts.quote: On 18 April 2019, 16.5 million people were enrolled to vote in Australian elections.

rules.quote: Avoid beginning a sentence with a string of numbers and dates
rules.violation_condition: a sentence beginning with an introductory phrase ending in a numeral and followed immediately by another numeral
rules.why: Candidate heading directly states the constraint tested by the Write this and Not this examples.

covers.quote: Set off non-essential clauses
Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.
If you can remove the clause and your sentence means the same thing, it’s non-essential and should go between commas.
Non-essential clauses are also called ‘non-restrictive’ or ‘non-defining’ clauses.

examples.note: Non-essential clause enclosed in a pair of commas.

parts.quote: The business report, which the manager had edited, explained the agency’s strategy.

examples.note: Non-essential supplementary information enclosed in commas.

rules.quote: Use commas around clauses that add information but aren’t essential to the meaning of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: a non-essential (non-restrictive) clause not set off by commas, or an essential (restrictive) clause enclosed in commas
when: Applies to non-essential (non-restrictive, non-defining) clauses.
Do not use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.
rules.why: G-2 combines non-essential vs essential clause conditions; E-1 treats meaning contrast pair as compliant.

covers.quote: Use commas with the phrase ‘for example’
If ‘for example’ begins a sentence, it is an introductory phrase. Follow it with a comma.
If you’re introducing a bullet list after ‘for example’, use a colon.

examples.note: Surrounded by commas within sentence.

parts.quote: Some colours, for example, are difficult for people with colour blindness to distinguish.

examples.note: Followed by a comma when beginning a sentence.

green
orange

blue

rules.quote: Generally, use a comma before and after the phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: the phrase 'for example' used within a sentence without surrounding commas, at the start of a sentence without a following comma, or introducing a bullet list without a colon
when: The phrase 'for example' appears within a sentence (surround with a pair of commas).
The phrase 'for example' begins a sentence (follow with a comma).
The phrase 'for example' introduces a bullet list (use a colon instead of a comma).
rules.why: G-2 combines sentence placement conditions; E-3 groups bullet list lead-in and items as one example.

when: Using Latin shortened forms such as 'e.g.' and 'i.e.'.

covers.quote: Place commas between principal clauses joined together with a conjunction
If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
The exception to this rule is when you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.

examples.note: Comma placed before conjunction because clauses have different subjects.

parts.quote: The Senate debated the Bill at length, but the party whips eventually called for a vote.

examples.note: No comma before conjunction because two clauses share the same subject.

parts.quote: The company closed its Perth office and sacked the chief financial officer.

examples.note: Commas used when more than two principal clauses share the same subject.

parts.quote: The company closed its Perth office, sacked the chief financial officer, and opened a branch in Singapore.

rules.quote: Use commas to connect 2 or more principal clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’, ‘so’).
rules.violation_condition: two principal clauses with different subjects joined by a coordinating conjunction without a comma before the conjunction, or two clauses with the same subject separated by an unnecessary comma before the conjunction
when: Two or more principal clauses are joined by a coordinating conjunction ('and', 'or', 'but', 'so').
If clauses have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
If two clauses share the same subject, do not insert a comma before the conjunction.
If more than two principal clauses share the same subject, use commas to separate them.
rules.why: Explicitly cited in policy G-2 as one rule consolidating shared vs different subject conditions.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas to ‘splice’ sentences

examples.note: Comma splice: two stand-alone clauses joined only with a comma.

rules.quote: Don’t use a comma to link 2 stand-alone sentences unless you use a coordinating conjunction.
rules.violation_condition: a comma used to link two independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction
when: Two stand-alone sentences (independent clauses) are linked.
rules.why: G-4 quotes body sentence; Correct and Incorrect demonstrate comma splice violation.

covers.quote: Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas
This rule applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists. Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.

examples.note: Items in sentence list separated by commas.

parts.quote: The delegation visited Brisbane, Canberra and Adelaide.

examples.note: Items in sentence list separated by commas.

when: Applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists.
Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.
rules.why: Explicitly cited in policy G-4; body instruction preferred over candidate heading.

covers.quote: Avoid using a comma before the last item in the list.
If the last item combines 2 words or phrases with the word ‘and’, use a comma before that final item. This use of the comma is known as the ‘Oxford comma’ or ‘serial comma’.
The Oxford comma can prevent ambiguity in complex sentence lists. For example, use the Oxford comma before the last item if you’re using a defining phrase applicable only to that final item.

examples.note: Oxford comma used because final item combines two words with 'and'.

parts.quote: The industries most affected are retail trade, wholesale trade, and accommodation and food services.

examples.note: Oxford comma omitted because defining phrase applies to all items.

parts.quote: The analysis outlined demand for barley, wheat and hay for stockfeed.

Use an Oxford comma if the last item combines 2 words or phrases with 'and'.
Use an Oxford comma to prevent ambiguity in complex sentence lists.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates Oxford comma restriction and its ambiguity-preventing exceptions; E-1 keeps contrast pairs compliant.

covers.quote: Separate adjectives of the same type
When writing strings of adjectives, use a set order – evaluative, descriptive, then definitive.
Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.

when: Adjectives in a string are of the same type (use commas).
Adjectives in a string are of different types (do not use commas).
Adjective strings should follow the order: evaluative, descriptive, then definitive.
rules.why: G-2 unifies same-type and different-type adjective rules; G-4 quotes body sentence.

covers.quote: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits
Don’t use a space between the digits, because screen readers can read them as separate numbers.
When you are using numbers of 1,000 or more, use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).
Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.
Don’t use commas in postcodes or dates.

covers.quote: Show direct speech or quoted material using commas
If an attribution comes after a quotation, use a comma at the end of the quotation and before the quotation mark.
If the quotation is broken into 2 parts, the second part should follow a full stop rather than a comma.
If the quotation ends the sentence, end it with the original punctuation of the quotation.

covers.quote: Place commas between principal clauses joined together with a conjunction
If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
The exception to this rule is when you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.

examples.note: Comma placed before conjunction because clauses have different subjects.

parts.quote: The Senate debated the Bill at length, but the party whips eventually called for a vote.

examples.note: No comma before conjunction because two clauses share the same subject.

parts.quote: The company closed its Perth office and sacked the chief financial officer.

examples.note: Commas used when more than two principal clauses share the same subject.

parts.quote: The company closed its Perth office, sacked the chief financial officer, and opened a branch in Singapore.

tags.violation_condition: two principal clauses with different subjects joined by a coordinating conjunction without a comma before the conjunction, or two clauses with the same subject separated by an unnecessary comma before the conjunction

when: Two or more principal clauses are joined by a coordinating conjunction ('and', 'or', 'but', 'so').
If clauses have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
If two clauses share the same subject, do not insert a comma before the conjunction.
If more than two principal clauses share the same subject, use commas to separate them.
rules.why: Explicitly cited in policy G-2 as one rule consolidating shared vs different subject conditions.

anchor.quote: Don’t use a comma to link 2 stand-alone sentences unless you use a coordinating conjunction.
anchor.suffix: This kind of error is called a

covers.quote: Don’t use commas to ‘splice’ sentences

examples.note: Clauses linked with a comma and a coordinating conjunction.

parts.quote: The report was finished last week, but the minister has not approved its release.

examples.note: Comma splice: two stand-alone clauses joined only with a comma.

parts.quote: The report was finished last week, the minister has not approved its release.

tags.violation_condition: a comma used to link two independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction

when: Two stand-alone sentences (independent clauses) are linked.
rules.why: G-4 quotes body sentence; Correct and Incorrect demonstrate comma splice violation.

anchor.quote: Use commas between items in a sentence list.
anchor.suffix: Avoid using a comma before the

covers.quote: Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas
This rule applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists. Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.

examples.note: Items in sentence list separated by commas.

parts.quote: The delegation visited Brisbane, Canberra and Adelaide.

examples.note: Items in sentence list separated by commas.

parts.quote: The consultation involved businesses, sole traders and not-for-profits.

examples.note: Adjective phrases in sentence list separated by commas.

parts.quote: The applicant was willing to learn, eager to work and well prepared.

tags.violation_condition: items in a sentence list not separated by commas, or a bullet list item punctuated with a comma

when: Applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists.
Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.
rules.why: Explicitly cited in policy G-4; body instruction preferred over candidate heading.

anchor.quote: Restrict the use of the Oxford comma

covers.prefix: tween items in a sentence list.
covers.quote: Avoid using a comma before the last item in the list.
If the last item combines 2 words or phrases with the word ‘and’, use a comma before that final item. This use of the comma is known as the ‘Oxford comma’ or ‘serial comma’.
The Oxford comma can prevent ambiguity in complex sentence lists. For example, use the Oxford comma before the last item if you’re using a defining phrase applicable only to that final item.

examples.note: Oxford comma used because final item combines two words with 'and'.

parts.quote: The industries most affected are retail trade, wholesale trade, and accommodation and food services.

examples.note: Oxford comma omitted because defining phrase applies to all items.

parts.quote: The analysis outlined demand for barley, wheat and hay for stockfeed.

examples.note: Oxford comma used because defining phrase applies only to final item.

parts.quote: The analysis outlined demand for barley, wheat, and hay for stockfeed.

tags.violation_condition: a comma placed before the final conjunction in a sentence list where it is not needed to prevent ambiguity or separate a complex final item

when: Avoid using a comma before the last item in a sentence list.
Use an Oxford comma if the last item combines 2 words or phrases with 'and'.
Use an Oxford comma to prevent ambiguity in complex sentence lists.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates Oxford comma restriction and its ambiguity-preventing exceptions; E-1 keeps contrast pairs compliant.

anchor.quote: Use commas in strings of adjectives of the same type (for example, a string of descriptive adjectives).

covers.quote: Separate adjectives of the same type
When writing strings of adjectives, use a set order – evaluative, descriptive, then definitive.
Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.

examples.note: Commas separate descriptive adjectives of the same type.

parts.quote: This is an ethical, profitable, efficient organisation.

examples.note: Commas separate evaluative adjectives of the same type.

parts.quote: They were a happy, caring, devoted workforce.

examples.note: No commas between adjectives of different types.

parts.quote: My new black felt-tip pen splattered ink everywhere.

examples.note: No commas between adjectives of different types.

parts.quote: We found some used French tennis balls left over from a training day.

tags.violation_condition: a string of adjectives of the same type not separated by commas, or a string of adjectives of different types separated by commas

when: Adjectives in a string are of the same type (use commas).
Adjectives in a string are of different types (do not use commas).
Adjective strings should follow the order: evaluative, descriptive, then definitive.
rules.why: G-2 unifies same-type and different-type adjective rules; G-4 quotes body sentence.

anchor.quote: Numbers with 4 or more digits (starting from 1,000) need a comma.
anchor.suffix: Use commas for numerals in text

covers.quote: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits
Don’t use a space between the digits, because screen readers can read them as separate numbers.
When you are using numbers of 1,000 or more, use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).
Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.
Don’t use commas in postcodes or dates.

examples.note: Comma used in 4-digit number.

parts.quote: The agency handles around 6,500 complaints each year.

examples.note: Space used instead of a comma in 4-digit number.

parts.quote: The agency handles around 6 500 complaints each year.
parts.suffix: [This can be read as the number

examples.note: Thousands comma used.
Thousands comma used.
Thousands commas used.
No comma used to the right of the decimal point.
Comma used to the left of decimal point but not to the right.
No comma in a year.

parts.quote: The year was 2020.

examples.note: No comma in a postcode.

parts.quote: The office was in postcode area 6500.

tags.violation_condition: a number of 4 or more digits written without a thousands comma, other than a year or postcode or the digits after a decimal point

when: Applies to numerals of 1,000 or more in text and tables.
Do not use a space between digits instead of a comma.
Do not use commas to the right of a decimal point.
Do not use commas in postcodes or dates.
rules.why: Prompt policy defines this exact violation condition; G-2 folds number exceptions into when.

anchor.quote: Introduce directly quoted speech with a comma.
anchor.suffix: Use the comma in combination wi

covers.quote: Show direct speech or quoted material using commas
If an attribution comes after a quotation, use a comma at the end of the quotation and before the quotation mark.
If the quotation is broken into 2 parts, the second part should follow a full stop rather than a comma.
If the quotation ends the sentence, end it with the original punctuation of the quotation.

examples.note: Comma introduces directly quoted speech.

parts.quote: She said, ‘It’s time to start work.’

examples.note: Comma introduces directly quoted speech.

parts.quote: The Prime Minister said, ‘I’m calling a half-Senate election.’

examples.note: Comma precedes attribution and sits inside quotation mark.

parts.quote: ‘It’s time to start work,’ she said.

examples.note: Comma precedes attribution and sits inside quotation mark.

parts.quote: ‘I’m calling a half-Senate election for Saturday 15 August,’ the Prime Minister said.

examples.note: Full stop rather than comma introduces the second part of a broken quotation.

parts.quote: ‘It’s time to start work,’ she said. ‘We have a lot to do.’

examples.note: Full stop rather than comma introduces the second part of a broken quotation.

parts.quote: ‘I’m calling a half-Senate election,’ the Prime Minister said. ‘It will be held on Saturday 15 August.’

examples.note: Sentence ends with original punctuation of quotation.

parts.quote: She said, ‘It’s time to start work.’

examples.note: Sentence ends with question mark from original quotation.

parts.quote: She asked, ‘Is it time to start work?’

tags.violation_condition: directly quoted speech introduced without a comma, or attribution following a quote without a comma before the closing quotation mark

when: Introducing directly quoted speech (place comma before quotation mark).
Attribution comes after a quotation (place comma inside quotation mark before attribution).
Quotation is broken into 2 parts (second part follows a full stop rather than a comma).
Quotation ends the sentence (end with original punctuation of the quotation).
rules.why: G-2 combines quotation attribution conditions into one rule; G-4 quotes body sentence.
